claims.text: A 55-year-old man had vomited after eating, with upper abdominal pain, distending pain and bloating. Vomitus was white digestive juice, about 5 mL each time. He had no fever, night sweats, cough, expectoration, chest tightness or shortness of breath, no chronic disease history, and a negative physical examination. Gastroscopy at a local hospital on February 1, 2024 suggested gastric stromal tumors.

claims.text: Laboratory tests showed CRP 97.39 mg/L and procalcitonin 4.63 ng/mL. After admission, abdominal CT showed marked thickening of the gastric wall at the fundus-body junction and gastric angle with nodular protrusions into the lumen, sizes of approximately 76 x 39 x 51 mm and 72 x 58 x 46 mm, moderate progressive enhancement, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes, the largest 12 mm in short diameter. The preoperative diagnosis was a gastric stromal tumor, which the authors call a misdiagnosis.

claims.text: After excluding surgical contraindications, laparoscopic partial gastrectomy under general anesthesia was performed on February 26, 2024. Pathology confirmed a spindle cell tumor of gastric origin consistent with schwannoma, S100 and SOX-10 positive and CD34, CD117, DOG-1, SMA and desmin negative, with Ki67 below 10%. The authors described multiple gastric schwannomas and considered schwannomatosis NOS, without molecular or genetic testing.
